doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Teaching by ear: Freddie Hubbard, Blue Note players, Doc Russell gigs
summary: Vega slows students down and tells them to learn by ear, recalling Freddie Hubbard's comment, the Blue Note community, and learning 30-odd tunes by ear with Doc Russell and James Spaulding.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well with all that in mind, your ear learning and your ability to play well and fit into the music, does this have ramifications for how you teach your students?

I’ve had students who come to me with things they’ve learned from other teachers or perhaps on the Internet and they ask about certain harmonic things that I never use. And so I’m wondering how to deal with that?

Well what happens is these kids are also getting on the Internet and getting tons of information and getting there’s — I think it’s sensory overload, the amount of information that they can get. So I slow them down and I just tell them okay, let’s slow down and I let them know, you know, you’re going to have to learn how to play by ear. You’re going to have to. I tell them you’ve got to learn all these scales, you’re going to learn all these patterns, you’re going to get the sound of this under your fingers. When it comes down to you playing the music, if you can’t immerse yourself in the sound of the music and allow yourself to play, you’re not really playing. I remember a conversation I had with Freddie Hubbard where Freddie tells me, he tells me, Freddie was funny, he’d go, “Ray, they’re asking me why did I play such-and-such a thing on such-and-such a chord on “One Finger Snap.” And he goes, “Man at that time we were playing by ear.” And I figured, and I didn’t question him about that, I just listened to him and I went of course they were because they were first of all, these guys were a community of players in New York. They were living in New York at the time, a lot of them. So they were a community of players, so think about who his contemporaries were at the time that he was hanging out with. He was hanging out with Coltrane, he was hanging out with Eric Dolphy, he was hanging out with James Spaulding, Joe Henderson, those are just some of the saxophone players, Wayne Shorter, Cedar Walton, McCoy Tyner, Herbie, and on and on and on and on, and you think about these great minds and how they’re coming © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

together for these Blue Note sessions which they really just — these were not working bands. They got together, looked at the music and went in. But at that point they were speaking to each other in such a highly sophisticated fashion that they could hear through things. They could hear through things. So what I tell the students is I tell them you’re not going to be able to play freely if all you’re going to have is that piece of music in front of you and looking at the chord progressions to figure out what you need to play against. You’ve got to get to the point where you hear what the changes are. Because that’s what I learned from playing by ear. I can go to a jam session and they could be playing “All the Things You Are” and I knew exactly where they were at every given moment. I wasn’t going to be able to recite the chord progressions to you but I could hear where they were and I could hear the melody. But that was the whole thing with Doc Russell’s — we would go out and do gigs and by the time, you know maybe five or six months into my hanging out with them I learned like 30, 35 tunes all by ear, that I would play with his band. And of course I was young, I was a young kid so I was going to sound like a young kid, but they never once mentioned one chord progression to me. They never did that. It was just like check it out, listen to it. And one of the guys that was playing with Doc that would come to play many times with Doc was James Spaulding. James Spaulding from Indianapolis of the fame of the Freddie Hubbard’s group, played with McCoy Tyner, played with all these great recordings on Blue Note Records. But Spaulding would be there and they’d just go, “Yeah, try it again, try it again, try it again.” He never sat there, “Hey man that’s a minor 2-5 and you’ve got to play this.” He didn’t do that. Don’t get me wrong, I think it’s important to learn the mathematics of it, but I think a lot of kids, the biggest problem with what a lot of kids are doing is that they’re trying to play this music by learning the math about it but they’re not really immersing themselves in the actual music. They’re not listening to the recordings. This is part of my discussion in my Jazz History classes. I walk in front and I pull out my thing and I go, “This is the problem, folks. Everybody here has 5,000 tunes on them and they listen to the first 20 seconds of one tune and they go to another one, and nobody’s listening to music from the beginning to the end and of course now with the shuffle option that you have in playing music, you’re not even listening to a recording from beginning to end. You know? You put down “Blues and the Abstract Truth” Oliver Nelson. Let it play through. Turn it over. Let it play through, turn it over again. And that’s how we immersed ourselves in the sound of the music around us.
